newsitem.title: USA: Hatcheries, charities seek salmon-giveaway plan.
newsitem.headline: Hatcheries, charities seek salmon-giveaway plan.

text.p: Alaska's waters are so choked with salmon that commercial fishermen and hatchery operators have had to throw hundreds of thousands of fish away, officials said Wednesday.

To reduce the waste by channelling some of the fish to food banks in a coordinated plan was the subject of a two-day meeting of salmon hatchery operators, charity managers and state officials held Tuesday and Wednesday.

Low prices and high production resulted in an unmarketable excess of 2.5 million salmon, according to preliminary state figures. The glut is most troublesome for low-priced pink salmon, sometimes called humpback salmon, the most plentiful of Alaska's five salmon species.

Because the problem is likely to persist, the state needs a strategy to give away as much of the excess fish as possible at the lowest cost, said Geron Bruce, deputy commissioner of the Alaska Department of Fish and Game.

"Given the current and likely future outlook for the salmon industry, with high production exceeding demand, lower quality salmon are going to continue to be pushed out of some of the traditional market niches," said Bruce, who attended the two-day meeting.

The session was promoted by activists' outrage that the state this summer issued special permits allowing hatchery operators to rip marketable roe out of harvested salmon, then dump the unmarketable carcasses at sea.

"If you or I killed a salmon, took its eggs, threw it on a streambank or in a trash can, we would be guilty of wanton waste and go to jail," said Judy Sehn, a volunteer with the Anchorage-based food giveway group EARTH.

Michael O'Callaghan, an Anchorage political gadfly and founder of EARTH, lost 45 pounds in a summer hunger strike over the practice. "I have a difficult time communicating with people who are not hungry," he said at the meeting.
He also filed lawsuits to block the practice, including a complaint against the Department of Fish and Game filed Wednesday.
O'Callaghan said EARTH has given away about 1.2 million pounds of food since 1991, including hundreds of thousands of the spawned-out "brood stock" pink salmon rejected by Alaskans.

For example, EARTH gave away more than 40,000 salmon in Portland in September -- "spawned-out, slimy humpies that we Alaskans are so picky about, that we want to know if there's any water marks on it before we eat it" -- in just 30 minutes, he said.

Although it did not use the low-quality brood stock, Second Harvest, a cooperative of nearly 200 food banks, distributed about 1 million pounds of excess Alaska salmon to food banks as far away as New York and Texas, said Debra Keegan, marketing manager for the Chicago-based group.
"We feel that we could go from distributing 1 million pounds to distributing 12 million pounds, if we could get some assistance fro mthe government in providing processing costs," Keegan said.
But hatchery operators and fish processors said they fear a flood of unpalatable, low-quality fish will further harm the belagured Alaska salmon industry.
